content:
Psoriatic arthritis causes painful, swollen joints in some people who have psoriasis. Early signs include a whole finger or toe swelling up like a sausage, heel or foot pain, stiffness in the morning, and pitted or lifting nails. It can start before skin psoriasis appears. If you notice these, see your GP, because early treatment can prevent joint damage.

Who gets it

Psoriatic arthritis most often starts between the ages of 30 and 50, but it can happen at any age. Many people with psoriasis never develop it. Having a close relative with psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis increases the chance.

Related reading: Rheumatoid Arthritis Treatment, Hip Arthritis Symptoms UK: Signs, Diagnosis and Treatment Options, Signs of Rheumatoid Arthritis in Early Stages

Early signs to look out for

  • dactylitis: a whole finger or toe that becomes swollen, red and painful
  • enthesitis: pain where tendons attach to bone, such as the back of the heel or the sole of the foot
  • joint pain and swelling, often in a patchy pattern and not always on both sides
  • morning stiffness that lasts more than 30 minutes
  • nail changes: pitting, ridges, discolouration or the nail lifting off the nail bed
  • back or buttock pain that is worse with rest and better with movement
  • tiredness
  • eye inflammation (uveitis): a red, painful eye with blurred vision, which needs urgent same-day assessment

Symptoms often come and go in flares.

Getting diagnosed

There is no single test. Your GP will examine you and may arrange blood tests and X-rays. Most people with psoriatic arthritis have a negative test for rheumatoid factor. NICE recommends that people with psoriasis have an annual check for signs of psoriatic arthritis. If inflammatory arthritis is suspected, your GP should refer you to a rheumatologist.

Treatment

The aim is to control inflammation, relieve pain and protect joints.

  • Anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIDs) can ease pain and stiffness in mild cases.
  • Steroid injections into a swollen joint can settle a flare.
  • DMARDs such as methotrexate, sulfasalazine or leflunomide are used for ongoing inflammation. Methotrexate may also help the skin.
  • Biologics and targeted therapies are used if DMARDs are not enough. These include anti-TNF, anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 medicines and JAK inhibitors. NICE sets the criteria for NHS use.

Many treatments help both skin and joints, so your rheumatology and dermatology teams may work together.

Living well with psoriatic arthritis

  • Exercise regularly. It keeps joints flexible and muscles strong. Swimming, cycling and walking are good choices.
  • Manage your weight. Extra weight can increase inflammation and may reduce how well some treatments work.
  • Stop smoking and keep alcohol within limits, especially if you take methotrexate.
  • Look after your heart. Psoriatic disease raises cardiovascular risk, so have blood pressure and cholesterol checked.
  • Foot care. A podiatrist can help with heel pain, insoles and nail problems.
  • Fatigue and mood. These are common. Talk to your team if they are affecting your life.

What the future looks like

With modern treatment, many people with psoriatic arthritis keep working and doing what they enjoy. The key is getting diagnosed early, staying in touch with your team and reporting flares or side effects promptly.

Questions to ask your GP or rheumatologist

  • Could my joint, heel or nail symptoms be psoriatic arthritis?
  • Do I need a referral to rheumatology?
  • What treatment will help both my skin and my joints?
  • What blood tests will I need while on treatment?
  • Who do I contact if I have a flare?

Bring photos of swollen fingers or toes if the swelling has gone down by the time of your appointment. They can help your doctor understand what you are experiencing. A short diary of when symptoms started and how long morning stiffness lasts is also useful.

When to get urgent help

Call 999 or go to A&E if you have:

  • a joint that suddenly becomes hot, red, swollen and very painful, especially if you feel feverish or unwell (this can be a joint infection)
  • chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or signs of a stroke such as face drooping, arm weakness or slurred speech

Contact NHS 111 or your GP the same day if symptoms are getting worse quickly, you cannot put weight on a leg, or you are worried and not sure where to go. If you are under a rheumatology team, use their advice line for flares and medicine questions.
